newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean gold trade jumps as firms probe loopholes.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean gold trade jumps as firms probe loopholes.

text.p: South Korea's gold transshipment trade appears to be rising as local companies exploit a loophole in government rules designed to prevent last year's favoured deferred-payment practice, traders said on Monday.

On Friday, an official with the central Bank of Korea said South Korea's gold imports had surged 25.6 percent to 304 tonnes for the first six months of this year from 242 tonnes in the same period last year.
The official said exports for the first half rose 23.9 percent to 285 tonnes from 230 tonnes in the same year ago period.

In value terms, imports over the period totalled $3.40 billion, compared to $3.08 billion a year ago. Exports for the first six months totalled $3.16 billion, compared to $2.91 billion a year earlier, the official said.
Traders said the rise indicated that local bullion houses had found several ways to get around rules, put into effect last July, aimed at curbing South Korea's once-booming gold transshipment trade.
Those rules shortened importers' deferred-payment period on imports to 30 days from 120 days, effectively limiting importers' arbitrage profits.

Previously, bullion houses had imported huge amounts of gold on 90-day deferred payments, then immediately exported it and parked the proceeds in high interest-bearing domestic money market instruments.
They reaped huge profits from arbitrage between local interest rates of more than 12 percent and London Interbank Offered Rates of around six percent.
Now, however, companies are requiring advance payments of as much as 120 days on gold exports, traders said.
"Several domestic bullion houses are currently seen using the advanced payment by overseas' buyers to get around the rules," said another local bullion trader.

The trader said some bullion houses were requiring advance payment of up to 120 days from foreign buyers. That, plus the current 30 days of deferred payments, would give the bullion houses control of funds for a maximum of 150 days.
However, the trader said the advanced payment scheme also had its limits.
In February, the limit was raised from 20 percent to 25 percent of each company's total sales turnover for the previous year, starting from July 1996 to June this year.
"Competition among major trading firms by the end of this period could also be another reason behind the rise in bullion trade," the trader said.
Another trader said some bullion houses were trying to raise current low margins by increasing both their gold imports and exports.

"A series of corporate collapses and financial woes since early this year has made it difficult for local companies to borrow from local banks and forced them to pay higher interest rates due to the banks' credit squeeze," a trader with a major trading house said.
Other traders said several local companies were also seen getting around the government crackdown on gold transshipment trade by setting up tie-up agreements with local refining companies.

Samsung Corp formed a tie-up with privately-owned German firm Heraeus Oriental Hitec Co Ltd in mid-April to build a refining plant to turn imported low grade gold into gold bars of more than 99.99 percent purity.
The plant has an annual capacity of 30 tonnes of refined gold bars.
Traders said Hyundai Corp also made a tie-up agreement with Korea Zinc for refining business from local market.
Hyundai was not immediately available for comment.
Korea Zinc Co Ltd and LG Metals Corp are South Korea's major gold producers.
They said gold imported for refining was still subject to a maximum 180 days deferred payment rule. If the gold is then exported, there is a three percent import tax rebate.
-- Seoul Newsroom (822) 727 5651
